Boil
BOYL
noun
From the Old English byl or byle, a swelling or sore, kin to the German Beule; unrelated in origin to the verb to boil, which comes through French from the Latin bullire. It renders the Hebrew shechin, an inflamed ulcer or burning sore.

Biblical Definition

The boil is an inflamed and burning ulcer of the flesh, and Scripture puts it in three places that must be held together. It is a plague upon Egypt: the ashes of the furnace became “a boil breaking forth with blains upon man, and upon beast” (Exo 9:9), until the magicians who had matched Moses trick for trick “could not stand before Moses because of the boils” (Exo 9:11) — the sorcerers driven from the field by their own skin. It is the affliction of the righteous man: Satan “smote Job with sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown” (Job 2:7), and Job scraped himself with a potsherd among the ashes. Mark what that verse establishes. The devil struck the blow, but he struck it only within the bounds the LORD had set, so that the boil of Job is at once a work of Satan and a providence of God, without contradiction and without excusing the tempter. And it is the sickness that God heals by means: Hezekiah lay dying, and “Isaiah said, Take a lump of figs. And they took and laid it on the boil, and he recovered” (2Ki 20:7). A word from the LORD had promised fifteen years; a poultice of figs was still applied. The promise did not make the figs superfluous, and the figs did not make the promise unnecessary.

Webster 1828 Definition

A tumor or inflamed swelling upon the flesh which suppurates; an angry sore or ulcer breaking forth upon the skin.

BOIL, a tumor upon the flesh, accompanied with inflammation and suppuration; an angry swelling or sore.

From Saxon byl, a swelling; the same word as the German Beule. Distinct from the verb to boil, Latin bullire.

The sixth plague of Egypt was a boil breaking forth with blains upon man and beast (Exo 9:9–11).

Job was smitten with sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown (Job 2:7).

Hezekiah’s boil was healed after a lump of figs was laid upon it at the prophet’s word (2Ki 20:7; Isa 38:21).

Key Scripture

Exo 9:9 — "And it shall become small dust in all the land of Egypt, and shall be a boil breaking forth with blains upon man, and upon beast, throughout all the land of Egypt."

Exo 9:11 — "And the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils; for the boil was upon the magicians, and upon all the Egyptians."

Job 2:7 — "So went Satan forth from the presence of the LORD, and smote Job with sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown."

2Ki 20:7 — "And Isaiah said, Take a lump of figs. And they took and laid it on the boil, and he recovered."

Modern Corruption

The boil of Job and the boil of Hezekiah together destroy the health-and-wealth doctrine: the most upright man in the East was covered with sores, and the king whom God promised to heal was still given a poultice.

expand to see more

The Word-of-Faith and health-and-wealth teachers — Kenyon, Hagin, Copeland, and the prosperity preachers who followed them — hold that bodily healing is guaranteed in the atonement and may be claimed on demand, so that continuing sickness proves a defect of faith in the sufferer. Job settles the question in two verses. The LORD Himself calls Job perfect and upright, one that feared God and eschewed evil, and it is precisely that man who is covered with boils from sole to crown. His friends preached the prosperity doctrine at him for thirty chapters, reasoning backward from his sores to his supposed secret sin, and God ended the book by telling Eliphaz that His wrath was kindled against them, for they had not spoken of Him the thing that was right. The apostolic record says the same: Paul’s thorn was not removed but answered with sufficient grace (2Co 12:7–9), Timothy kept his often infirmities and was told to take a little wine (1Ti 5:23), and Trophimus was left at Miletum sick (2Ti 4:20). A doctrine that cannot account for Job, Paul, Timothy, and Trophimus is not a doctrine of Scripture, and it is cruel at the bedside besides.

The opposite error is fatalism, and Hezekiah’s boil forbids that too. God had already sworn to add fifteen years to the king’s life; the outcome was fixed by divine decree and could not fail. And still Isaiah said, take a lump of figs and lay it on the boil. The Reformed doctrine of providence has always insisted that God ordains the end and the means together, so that the certainty of the end is the very reason to use the means, not an excuse to despise them. He who decreed that Hezekiah should live decreed the figs. So the believer prays and takes the medicine, trusts the LORD and calls the physician, and does both without the least embarrassment. Presumption says God will heal, so refuse the means; fatalism says God has decided, so the means are pointless; Scripture says the God who appoints the recovery appoints the poultice, and the sufferer is to use what is set before him and leave the issue with Him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

A burning ulcer of the flesh — plague upon Egypt, trial of Job, and the sickness God healed by means.

expand to see more

Boil — Saxon byl, a swelling; German Beule; not from Latin bullire.

Hebrew shechin, an inflamed and burning sore.

Egypt’s sixth plague drove the magicians from the field (Exo 9:11).

Satan smote Job with boils, but only within the bounds God had set (Job 2:7).

Hezekiah’s recovery was promised by God and applied with figs (2Ki 20:7).

Usage

"From the sole of his foot unto his crown — the measure of Job’s affliction, and of his patience."

"The magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils; the sorcerer is not exempt from the plague."

"Take a lump of figs: the promise of God and the use of means are not rivals."
